entries.7bda2d8f98d6b5da19b0bda156847b7422bb635c: <div sID="gen6012" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="2Sam.4" sID="2Sam.4"/> <div eID="gen6012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6013" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6014" type="x-p"/> When Abner was slain David was at a loss for a friend to perfect the reduction of those tribes that were yet in Ish-bosheth's interest. Which way to adopt for the accomplishment of it he could not tell; but here Providence brings it about by the removal of Ish-bosheth. I. Two of his own servants slew him, and brought his head to David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1-2Sam.4.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. David, instead of rewarding them, put them to death for what they had done, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.9-2Sam.4.12">ver. 9-12</reference>.
entries.6e542a6bf3ac18f30dda70512bcc7b1ecbd184f5: <div eID="gen6014" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6013" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ish-bosheth Slain by His Servants. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1048.)</title> <div sID="gen6015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when Saul's son heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, his hands were feeble, and all the Israelites were troubled. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Saul's son had two men <hi type="italic">that were</hi> captains of bands: the name of the one <hi type="italic">was</hi> Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon a Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin: (for Beeroth also was reckoned to Benjamin: <hi type="super">3</hi> And the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and were sojourners there until this day.) <hi type="super">4</hi> And Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son <hi type="italic">that was</hi> lame of <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame. And his name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Mephibosheth. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, went, and came about the heat of the day to the house of Ishbosheth, who lay on a bed at noon. <hi type="super">6</hi> And they came thither into the midst of the house, <hi type="italic">as though</hi> they would have fetched wheat; and they smote him under the fifth <hi type="italic">rib:</hi> and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped. <hi type="super">7</hi> For when they came into the house, he lay on his bed in his bedchamber, and they smote him, and slew him, and beheaded him, and took his head, and gat them away through the plain all night. <hi type="super">8</hi> And they brought the head of Ishbosheth unto David to Hebron, and said to the king, Behold the head of Ishbosheth the son of Saul thine enemy, which sought thy life; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath avenged my lord the king this day of Saul, and of his seed. <div eID="gen6015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6016" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The weakness of Saul's house. Still it grew weaker and weaker. 1. As for Ishbosheth, who was in possession of the throne, his hands were feeble, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1">v. 1</reference>. All the strength they ever had was from Abner's support, and now that he was dead he had no spirit left in him. Though Abner had, in a passion, deserted his interest, yet he hoped, by his means, to make good terms with David; but now even this hope fails him, and he sees himself forsaken by his friends and at the mercy of his enemies. All the Israelites that adhered to him were troubled and at a loss what to do, whether to proceed in their treaty with David or no. 2. As for Mephibosheth, who in the right of his father Jonathan had a prior title, his feet were lame, and he was unfit for any service, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">v. 4</reference>. He was but five years old when his father and grandfather were killed. His nurse, hearing of the Philistines' victory, was apprehensive that, in pursuit of it, they would immediately send a party to Saul's house, to cut off all that pertained to it, and would especially aim at her young master, who was now next heir to the crown. Under the apprehension of this, she fled with the child in her arms, to secure it either in some secret place where he could not be found, or in some strong place where he could not be got at; and, making more haste than good speed, she fell with the child, and by the fall some bone was broken or put out, and not well set, so that he was lame of it as long as he lived, and unfit either for court or camp. See what sad accidents children are liable to in their infancy, the effect of which may be felt by them, to their great uneasiness, all their days. Even the children of princes and great men, the children of good men, for such a one Jonathan was, children that are well tended, and have nurses of their own to take care of them, yet are not always safe. What reason have we to be thankful to God for the preservation of our limbs and senses to us, through the many perils of the weak and helpless state of infancy, and to own his goodness in giving his angels a charge concerning us, to bear us up in their arms, out of which there is no danger of falling, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.12">Ps. xci. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen6016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6017" type="x-p"/> II. The murder of Saul's son. We are here told, <div eID="gen6017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6018" type="x-p"/> 1. Who were the murderers: <hi type="italic">Baanah and Rechab,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.2-2Sam.4.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. They were own brothers, as Simeon and Levi, and partners in iniquity. They were or had been Ish-bosheth's own servants, employed under him, so much the more base and treacherous was it in them to do him a mischief. They were Benjamites, of his own tribe. They were of the city of Beeroth; for some reason which we cannot now account for care is here taken to let us know (in a parenthesis) that that city belonged to the lot of Benjamin, so we find (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.25">Josh. xviii. 25</reference>), but that the inhabitants, upon some occasion or other, perhaps upon the death of Saul, retired to Gittaim, another city which lay not far off in the same tribe, and was better fortified by nature, being situate (if we may depend upon Mr. Fuller's map) between the two rocks Bozez and Seneh. There the Beerothites were when this was written, and probably took root there, and never returned to Beeroth again, which made Beeroth, that had been one of the cities of the Gibeonites (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Josh. ix. 17</reference>), to be forgotten, and Gittaim to be famous long after, as we find, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.33">Neh. xi. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen6018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6019" type="x-p"/> 2. How the murder was committed, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5-2Sam.4.7">v. 5-7</reference>. See here, (1.) The slothfulness of Ish-bosheth. He lay upon his bed at noon. It does not appear that the country was at any time of the year so hot as to oblige the inhabitants to retire at noon, as we are told they do in Spain in the heat of summer; but Ishbosheth was a sluggish man, loved his ease and hated business: and when he should have been, at this critical juncture, at the head of his forces in the field, or at the head of his counsels in a treaty with David, he was lying upon his bed and sleeping, for his hands were feeble (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1">v. 1</reference>), and so were his head and heart. When those difficulties dispirit us which should rather invigorate us and sharpen our endeavours we betray both our crowns and lives. <hi type="italic">Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty and ruin.</hi> The idle soul is an easy prey to the destroyer. (2.) The treachery of Baanah and Rechab. They came into the house, under pretence of fetching wheat for the victualling of their regiments; and such was the plainness of those times that the king's corn-chamber and his bed-chamber lay near together, which gave them an opportunity, when they were fetching wheat, to murder him as he lay on the bed. We know not when and where death will meet us. When we lie down to sleep we are not sure but that we may sleep the sleep of death before we awake; nor do we know from what unsuspected hand a fatal stroke may come. Ish-bosheth's own men, who should have protected his life, took it away. <div eID="gen6019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6020" type="x-p"/> 3. The murderers triumphed in what they had done. As if they had performed some very glorious action, and the doing of it for David's advantage was enough not only to justify it, but to sanctify it, they made a present of Ish-bosheth's head to David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold the head of thy enemy,</hi> than which they thought nothing could be more acceptable to him; yea, and they made themselves instruments of God's justice, ministers to bear his sword, though they had no commission: <hi type="italic">The Lord hath avenged thee this day of Saul and of his seed.</hi> Not that they had any regard either to God or to David's honour; they aimed at nothing but to make their own fortunes (as we say) and to get preferment in David's court; but, to ingratiate themselves with him, they pretended a concern for his life, a conviction of his title, and a zealous desire to see him in full possession of the throne. Jehu pretended <hi type="italic">zeal for the Lord of hosts</hi> when an ambition to set up himself and his own family was the spring of his actions.
entries.bce0d3f96aa08f60bf46d1680c85490555f722fc: <div eID="gen6020" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ish-bosheth's Murderers Punished. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1048.)</title> <div sID="gen6021" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said unto them, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity, <hi type="super">10</hi> When one told me, saying, Behold, Saul is dead, thinking to have brought good tidings, I took hold of him, and slew him in Ziklag, who <hi type="italic">thought</hi> that I would have given him a reward for his tidings: <hi type="super">11</hi> How much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous person in his own house upon his bed? shall I not therefore now require his blood of your hand, and take you away from the earth? <hi type="super">12</hi> And David commanded his young men, and they slew them, and cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged <hi type="italic">them</hi> up over the pool in Hebron. But they took the head of Ishbosheth, and buried <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the sepulchre of Abner in Hebron. <div eID="gen6021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6022" type="x-p"/> We have here justice done upon the murderers of Ish-bosheth. <div eID="gen6022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6023" type="x-p"/> I. Sentence passed upon them. There needed no evidence, their own tongues witnessed against them; they were so far from denying the fact that they gloried in it. David therefore shows them the heinousness of the crime, and that blood called for blood from his hand, who was now the chief magistrate, and was by office the avenger of blood. And, perhaps, he was the more vigorous in the prosecution because for reasons of state he had spared Joab: "<hi type="italic">Shall I not require the blood of the slain at the hand of the slayers,</hi> and, since they cannot make restitution, take theirs instead of it?" Observe, 1. How he aggravates the crime, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.11">v. 11</reference>. Ish-bosheth was a righteous person, he had done them no wrong, nor designed them any. As to himself, David was satisfied that what opposition he gave him was not from malice, but mistake, from an idea he had of his own title to the crown, and the influence of others upon him, who urged him to put in for it. Note, Charity teaches us to make the best, not only of our friends, but of our enemies, and to think those may be righteous persons who yet, in some instances, do us wrong. I must not presently judge a man a bad man because I think him so to me. David owns Ish-bosheth an honest man, though he had created him a great deal of trouble unjustly. The manner of it much aggravated the crime. To slay him in his own house, which should have been his castle, and upon his bed, when he was in no capacity of making any opposition, this is treacherous and barbarous, and all that is base, and that which the heart of every man who is not perfectly lost to all honour and humanity will rise with indignation at the thought of. Assassinating is confessedly the most odious and villainous way of murdering. <hi type="italic">Cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly.</hi> 2. He quotes a precedent (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.10">v. 10</reference>): he had put him to death who had brought him the tidings of the death of Saul, because he thought it would be good tidings to David. Nothing is here said of that Amalekite's helping Saul to kill himself, only of his bringing the tidings of his death, by which it should seem that the story he told was upon enquiry found to be false, and that he lied against his own head. "Now" (says David) "did I treat him as a criminal, and not a favourite" (as he expected), "who brought me Saul's crown, and shall those be held guiltless that bring me Ish-bosheth's head?" 3. He ratifies the sentence with an oath (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the Lord liveth, who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity.</hi> He expresses himself thus resolutely, to prevent the making of any intercession for the criminals by those about him, and thus piously to intimate that his dependence was upon God for the putting of him in possession of the promised throne, and that he would not be beholden to any man to help him to it by any indirect or unlawful practices. God had redeemed him from all adversity hitherto, helped him over many a difficulty and through many a danger, and therefore he would depend upon him to crown and complete his own work. He speaks of his redemption from all adversity as a thing done, though he had many a storm yet before him, because he knew that he who had delivered would deliver. 4. Hereupon he signs a warrant for the execution of these men, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.12">v. 12</reference>. This may seem severe, when they intended him a kindness in what they did; but, (1.) He would thus show his detestation of the villany. When he heard that <hi type="italic">the Lord smote Nabal, he gave thanks</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.38-1Sam.25.39">1 Sam. xxv. 38, 39</reference>), <hi type="italic">for he is the God to whom vengeance belongeth;</hi> but, if wicked men smite Ish-bosheth, they deserve to die for taking God's work out of his hand. (2.) He would thus show his resentment of the great affront they put upon him in expecting that he should patronize and reward it; they could scarcely have done him a greater injury than thus to think him altogether such a one as themselves, one that cared not what blood he waded through to the crown. <div eID="gen6023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6024" type="x-p"/> II. Execution done. The murderers were put to death according to law, and their hands and feet were hung up; not their whole bodies, the law forbade that; but only their hands and feet, <hi type="italic">in terrorem—to frighten others,</hi> to be monuments of David's justice, and to make that to be taken notice of which would recommend him to the esteem of the people, as a man fit to rule, and that aimed not at his own preferment, nor had any enmity to the house of Saul, but only and sincerely designed the public welfare. But what a confusion was this to the two murderers! What a horrid disappointment! And such those will meet with who think to serve the interests of the Son of David by any immoral practices, by war and persecution, fraud and rapine, who, under colour of religion, murder princes, break solemn contracts, lay countries waste, <hi type="italic">hate their brethren, and cast them out, and say, Let the Lord be glorified, kill them, and think they do God good service.</hi> However men may canonize such methods of serving the church and the catholic cause, Christ will let them know, another day, that Christianity was not intended to destroy humanity; and those who thus think to merit heaven shall not escape the damnation of hell.  <chapter eID="2Sam.4"/> <div eID="gen6024" type="x-p"/>

entries.6dee843b3e4a3aaba13b04b4396804a3762c469d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2850"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen3922" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1">2Sa 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>. Baanah and Rechab Slay Ish-bosheth, and Bring His Head to Hebron.<div eID="gen3922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2850"/><hi type="bold">4. Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son that was lame of his feet--</hi>This is mentioned as a reason why, according to Oriental notions, he was considered unfit for exercising the duties of sovereignty. <div eID="gen3923" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a72ad44ff125fbb39015cd9176f41db8f36b8b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2851"/><div sID="gen3924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2851"/><hi type="bold">5-6. Rechab and Baanah went and came about the heat of the day to the house of Ish-bosheth, &c.--</hi>It is still a custom in the East to allow their soldiers a certain quantity of corn, together with some pay; and these two captains very naturally went to the palace the day before to fetch wheat, in order to distribute it to the soldiers, that it might be sent to the mill at the accustomed hour in the morning. <div eID="gen3924" type="x-p"/>
entries.07907d15040e98a14e3d8b12ee570906c9c140e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2852"/><div sID="gen3925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2852"/><hi type="bold">7. when they came into the house, he lay on his bed--</hi>Rechab and Baanah came in the heat of the day, when they knew that Ish-bosheth, their master, would be resting on his divan; and as it was necessary, for the reason just given, to have the corn the day before it was needed, their coming at that time, though it might be a little earlier than usual, created no suspicion, and attracted no notice [Harmer].<div eID="gen3925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gat them away through the plain--</hi>that is, the valley of the Jordan, through which their way lay from Mahanaim to Hebron. <div eID="gen3926" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8105559a2baafd90f7185cb4a4cc1a278c27039: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2853"/><div sID="gen3927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2853"/><hi type="bold">8. They brought the head of Ish-bosheth unto David ... and said, Behold the head of Ish-bosheth--</hi>Such bloody trophies of rebels and conspirators have always been acceptable to princes in the East, and the carriers have been liberally rewarded. Ish-bosheth being a usurper, the two assassins thought they were doing a meritorious service to David by removing the only existing obstacle to the union of the two kingdoms.<div eID="gen3927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3928" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.10-2Sam.4.12">2Sa 4:10-12</reference>. David Causes Them to Be Put to Death. <div eID="gen3928" type="x-p"/>
entries.3bee7f44eba4b4ba7106bdf4a408e131a5b638e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2854"/><div sID="gen3929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2854"/><hi type="bold">12. slew them, and cut off their hands and their feet--</hi>as the instruments in perpetrating their crime. The exposure of the mutilated remains was intended as not only a punishment of their crime, but also the attestation of David's abhorrence. <chapter eID="2Sam.4"/>

entries.79dac0e1db52e1cee6a5c54493960116dee2e794: <div eID="gen10771" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10772" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10772" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> Some account of Rechab and Baanah, two of Ish-bosheth's captains, and of Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1-2Sam.4.4">2Sam 4:1-4</reference>. Rechab and Baanah murder Ish-bosheth, and escape; and bring his head to David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5-2Sam.4.8">2Sam 4:5-8</reference>. David is greatly irritated, and commands them to be slain, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.9-2Sam.4.12">2Sam 4:9-12</reference>. <div eID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> All the Israelites were troubled - Abner was their great support; and on him they depended; for it appears that Ish-bosheth was a feeble prince, and had few of those qualities requisite for a sovereign.
entries.fa4843df83d0b6abe7d0868054623a5bcc404795: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> Captains of bands - Principes latronum, captains of banditti, says the Vulgate; the Syriac is the same. Whether Ish-bosheth kept bands of marauders, whose business it was to make sudden incursions into the country places, and carry off grain, provisions, cattle, etc., we know not; but such persons would be well qualified for the bloody work in which these two men were afterwards employed.
entries.72b50845b0771e3b1790ec29cc866ec3adae256c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> The Beerothites fled to Gittaim - Probably the same as Gath; as Ramathaim is the same as Ramah.
entries.84bec7581e39069cf55ef6318f014c0402cd51b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10779" type="x-p"/> He fell, and became lame - Dislocated his ankle, knee, or thigh; which was never after reduced; and thus he became lame. Lovely Jonathan! unfortunate in thy life, and in thy progeny.
entries.d55579c5a08b748cca11d3022d013bf1ab6d5f0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> Lay on a bed at noon - It is a custom in all hot countries to travel or work very early and very late, and rest at noonday, in which the heat chiefly prevails.
entries.0f77ab1f921342f08641e3c68b0f369795035192: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10781" type="x-p"/> As though they would have fetched wheat - The king's stores were probably near his own dwelling; and these men were accustomed to go thither for provisions for themselves, their cattle, and their men. This supposition which is natural, renders unnecessary all the emendations of Houbigant and others. <div eID="gen10781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10782" type="x-p"/> As these men were accustomed to bring wheat from these stores, from which it appears there was an easy passage to the king's chamber, (especially if we consider this a summer-house, as it most probably was), no man would suspect their present errand, as they were in the habit of going frequently to that place.
entries.66040b0a6124502f6413b14f89348cedaf9a8d78: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10783" type="x-p"/> They brought the head - unto David - They thought, as did the poor lying Amalekite, to ingratiate themselves with David by this abominable act.
entries.45a98578417406a97fde1c6fe0a6f0652705049c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10784" type="x-p"/> Who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity - This was, in David's case, a very proper view of the goodness and watchful providence of God towards him. His life was frequently in danger; murderers had often laid wait for it: but God, the living God, had always redeemed that life from all adversity; and called on him now to punish such evil-minded and blood-thirsty men.
entries.ef7a2ac58049ad30d67d41b5e30df151af3f4dc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> A reward for his tidings - Ὡ εδει με δουναι ευαγγελια, Septuagint. Here is a proof that ευαγγελιον, evangelium or gospel, signifies the reward which the bringer of good tidings is entitled to receive. See my preface to St. Matthew's Gospel.
entries.f66f7a2f30421fd30825d4c4ef60ef39d34ac4af: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10786" type="x-p"/> How much more - Here are several things which aggravated the guilt of those wicked men. <div eID="gen10786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10787" type="x-p"/> 1. Ish-bosheth was an innocent man, and therefore none could have any ground of quarrel against him. <div eID="gen10787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> 2. He was in his own house, which was his sanctuary, and none but the worst of men would disturb him there. <div eID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> 3. He was upon his bed, resting in the heat of the day, and so free from suspicion that he was not even attended by his guards, nor had he his doors secured. To take away the life of such a man, in such circumstances, whom also they professed to hold as their sovereign, was the most abandoned treachery.
entries.c8b41423d594a642214b22d2990260325a1674b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10790" type="x-p"/> And they slew them - None ever more richly deserved death; and by this act of justice, David showed to all Israel that he was a decided enemy to the destruction of Saul's family; and that none could lift up their hands against any of them without meeting with condign punishment. In all these cases I know not that it was possible for David to show more sincerity, or a stricter regard for justice.  <chapter eID="2Sam.4"/> <div eID="gen10790" type="x-p"/>

entries.b3bfe839b8241dd4d0da49d514e60728c9bdaac5: <hi type="italic">Murder of Ishbosheth.</hi> - 2Sa 4:1. When the son of Saul heard of the death of Abner, <hi type="italic">“his hands slackened,”</hi> i.e., he lost the power and courage to act as king, since Abner had been the only support of his throne. <hi type="italic">“And all Israel was confounded;”</hi> i.e., not merely alarmed on account of Abner’s death, but utterly at a loss what to do to escape the vengeance of David, to which Abner had apparently fallen a victim.
entries.ea2ea7be5074f0f4c0ae4effb22e2ebfc3cfc580: <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.2-2Sam.4.3">2Sa 4:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen4280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4281" type="x-p"/> Saul’s son had two leaders of military companies (for בן־שׁאוּל היוּ we must read שׁ לבן היוּ): the one was named <hi type="italic">Baanah</hi>, the other <hi type="italic">Rechab</hi>, sons of <hi type="italic">Rimmon</hi> the Beerothite, <hi type="italic">“of the sons of Benjamin,”</hi> i.e., belonging to them; <hi type="italic">“for Beeroth is also reckoned to Benjamin”</hi> (על, over, above, added to). <hi type="italic">Beeroth</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Bireh</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>), was close to the western frontier of the tribe of Benjamin, to which it is also reckoned as belonging in Jos 18:25. This remark concerning Beeroth in the verse before us, serves to confirm the statement that the Beerothites mentioned were Benjaminites; but that statement also shows the horrible character of the crime attributed to them in the following verses. Two men of the tribe of Benjamin murdered the son of Saul, the king belonging to their own tribe.
entries.aa87b038d6ea95be93bd54f8d5b811eac0510050: <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference> <div eID="gen4281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4282" type="x-p"/> Before the historian proceeds to describe what the two Beerothites did, he inserts a remark concerning Saul’s family, to show at the outset, that with the death of Ishbosheth the government of this family necessarily became extinct, as the only remaining descendant was a perfectly helpless cripple. He was a son of Jonathan, <hi type="italic">smitten</hi> (i.e., lamed) <hi type="italic">in his feet</hi>. He was five years old when the tidings came from Jezreel of Saul and Jonathan, i.e., of their death. His nurse immediately took him and fled, and on their hasty flight he fell and became lame. His name was <hi type="italic">Mephibosheth</hi> (according to Simonis, for בשׁת מפאה, destroying the idol); but in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.34">1Ch 8:34</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.40">1Ch 9:40</reference> he is called <hi type="italic">Meribbaal</hi> (Baal’s fighter), just as Ishbosheth is also called <hi type="italic">Eshbaal</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.8">2Sa 2:8</reference>). On his future history, see <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:1-13</reference>, 2Sa 16:1., and 2Sa 19:25.
entries.3d64c41fce1caf1e56159b434b4bd234d803cdd3: <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5">2Sa 4:5</reference> <div eID="gen4282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4283" type="x-p"/> The two sons of Rimmon went to Mahanaim, where Ishbosheth resided (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.8">2Sa 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.12">2Sa 2:12</reference>), and came in the heat of the day (at noon) into Ishbosheth’s house, when he was taking his mid-day rest.
entries.472cb8cfeca73a614edea589096e9c3d518d643b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.6">2Sa 4:6</reference> <hi type="italic">“And here they had come into the midst of the house, fetching wheat </hi>(i.e., under the pretext of fetching wheat, probably for the soldiers in their companies), <hi type="italic">and smote him in the abdomen; and Rechab and his brother escaped.”</hi> The first clause in this verse is a circumstantial clause, which furnishes the explanation of the way in which it was possible for the murderers to find their way to the king. The second clause continues the narrative, and ויּכּהוּ is attached to ויּבאוּ (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5">2Sa 4:5</reference>).<note placement="foot">The lxx thought it desirable to explain the possibility of Rechab and Baanah getting into the king’s house, and therefore paraphrased the sixth verse as follows: καὶ ἰδου ἡ θυρωρὸς τοῦ οἴκου ἐκάθαιρε πυροὺς καὶ ἐνύσταξε καὶ ἐκάθευδε, καὶ Ῥηχὰβ καὶ Βαανὰ οἱ ἄδελφοι διέλαθον (“and behold the doorkeeper of the house was cleaning wheat, and nodded and slept. And Rahab and Baana the brothers escaped, or went in secretly”). The first part of this paraphrase has been retained in the Vulgate, in the interpolation between <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5">2Sa 4:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.6">2Sa 4:6</reference> : <hi type="italic">et ostiaria domus purgans triticum obdormivit;</hi> whether it was copied by <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> from the Itala, or was afterwards introduced as a gloss into his translation. It is very evident that this clause in the Vulgate is only a gloss, from the fact that, in all the rest of <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.6">2Sa 4:6</reference>, Jerome has closely followed the Masoretic text, and that none of the other ancient translators found anything about a doorkeeper in his text. When Thenius, therefore, attempts to prove the “evident corruption of the Masoretic text,” by appealing to the “nonsense (<hi type="italic">Unsinn</hi>) of relating the murder of Ishbosheth and the flight of the murderers twice over, and in two successive verses (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.7">2Sa 4:7</reference>),” he is altogether wrong in speaking of the repetition as “nonsense” whereas it is simply tautology, and has measured the peculiarities of Hebrew historians by the standard adopted by our own. J. P. F. Königsfeldt has given the true explanation when he says: “The Hebrews often repeat in this way, for the purpose of adding something fresh, as for example, in this instance, their carrying off the head.” Comp. with this <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.22-2Sam.3.23">2Sa 3:22-23</reference>, where the arrival of Joab is mentioned twice, viz., in two successive verses; or <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.3">2Sa 5:1-3</reference>, where the assembling of the tribes of Israel at Hebron is also referred to a second time, - a repetition at which Thenius himself has taken no offence, - and many other passages of the same kind.</note>
entries.db27ce430747d2f7e61bec38eacf4813db5c48ff: <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.7-2Sam.4.8">2Sa 4:7-8</reference> <hi type="italic">Punishment of the murderers by David.</hi> - 2Sa 4:7. As the thread of the narrative was broken by the explanatory remarks in <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.6">2Sa 4:6</reference>, it is resumed here by the repetition of the words וגו ויּבאוּ: <hi type="italic">“They came into the house, as he lay upon his bed in his bed-chamber, and smote him, and slew him,”</hi> for the purpose of attaching the account of the further progress of the affair, viz., that they cut off his head, took it and went by the way of the Arabah (the valley of the Jordan: see <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.29">2Sa 2:29</reference>) the whole night, and brought the head of Ishbosheth unto David to Hebron with these words: “Behold (= there thou hast) the head of Ishbosheth, the son of Saul thine enemy, who sought thy life; and thus hath Jehovah avenged my lord the king this day upon Saul and his seed.” No motive is assigned for this action. But there can be little doubt that it was no other than the hope of obtaining a great reward from David. Thus they presumed “to spread the name of God and His providence as a cloak and covering over their villany, as the wicked are accustomed to do” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi>).
entries.09bb8c0a81db6f3d0f05041694ea64192e7b0bbf: <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.9-2Sam.4.11">2Sa 4:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen4283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4284" type="x-p"/> But David rewarded them very differently from what they had expected. He replied, <hi type="italic">“As Jehovah liveth, who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity, the man who told me, Behold, Saul is dead, and thought he was a messenger of good to me, I seized and slew at Ziklag</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.14-2Sam.1.15">2Sa 1:14-15</reference>), <hi type="italic">to give him a reward for his news: how much more when wicked men have murdered a righteous man in his house upon his bed, should I not require his blood at your hand, and destroy you from the earth?”</hi> The several parts of this reply are not closely linked together so as to form one period, but answer to the excited manner in which they were spoken. There is first of all the oath, <hi type="italic">“As truly as Jehovah liveth,”</hi> and the clause appended, <hi type="italic">“who redeemed my soul,”</hi> in which the thought is implied that David did not feel it necessary to get rid of his enemies by the commission of crimes. After this (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.10">2Sa 4:10</reference>) we have an allusion to his treatment of the messenger who announced Saul’s death to him, and pretended to have slain him in order that he might obtain a good reward for his tidings. כּי, like ὅτι, simply introduces the address. בּעיניו ... המּגּיד is placed at the head absolutely, and made subordinate to the verb by בו after ואחזה. לתתּי־לו, <hi type="italic">“namely, to give him.”</hi> עשׁר is employed to introduce the explanation, like our <hi type="italic">“namely”</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §338, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). בּשׂרה, good news, here <hi type="italic">“the reward of news.”</hi> The main point follows in <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.11">2Sa 4:11</reference>, beginning with כּי אף, <hi type="italic">“how much more”</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §354, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.), and is introduced in the form of a climax. The words משׁכּבו ... אנשׁים are also written absolutely, and placed at the head: “men have slain,” for “how much more in this instance, when wicked men have slain.” <hi type="italic">“Righteous”</hi> (<hi type="italic">zaddik</hi>), i.e., not guilty of any wicked deed or crime. The assumption of the regal power, which Abner had forced upon Ishbosheth, was not a capital crime in the existing state of things, and after the death of Saul; and even if it had been, the sons of Rimmon had no right to assassinate him. David’s sentence then follows: <hi type="italic">“And now that this is the fact, that ye have murdered a righteous man, should I not,”</hi> etc. בּער, to destroy by capital punishment, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">Deu 13:6</reference>, etc. דּם בּקּשׁ (=דּם דּרשׁ, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.5">Gen 9:5</reference>), to require the blood of a person, i.e., to take blood-revenge.
entries.813004df81ee374fd6ec8e0a5d77745321f33c2c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.12">2Sa 4:12</reference> <div eID="gen4284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4285" type="x-p"/> David then commanded his servant to slay the murderers, and also to make the punishment more severe than usual. <hi type="italic">“They cut off their hands and feet,”</hi> - the hands with which they had committed the murder, and the feet which had run for the reward, - <hi type="italic">“and hanged the bodies by the pool at Hebron”</hi> for a spectacle and warning, that others might be deterred from committing similar crimes (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.21.22">Deu 21:22</reference>; J. H. Michaelis). In illustration of the fact itself, we may compare the similar course pursued by Alexander towards the murderer of king Darius, as described in Justin’s history (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.6">2Sa 12:6</reference>) and Curtius (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.5">2Sa 7:5</reference>). They buried Ishbosheth’s head in Abner’s grave at Hebron. Thus David acted with strict justice in this case also, not only to prove to the people that he had neither commanded nor approved of the murder, but from heartfelt abhorrence of such crimes, and to keep his conscience void of offence towards God and towards man. II. The Government of David Over All Israel in the Time of Its Strength And Glory - 2 Samuel 5 <div eID="gen4285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4286" type="x-p"/> After the death of Ishbosheth, David was anointed in Hebron by all the tribes as king over the whole of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.5">2Sa 5:1-5</reference>). He then proceeded to attack the Jebusites in Jerusalem, conquered their fortress Zion, and made Jerusalem the capital of his kingdom; fortifying it still further, and building a palace in it (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6-2Sam.5.16">2Sa 5:6-16</reference>), after he had twice inflicted a defeat upon the Philistines (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.17-2Sam.5.25">2Sa 5:17-25</reference>). But in order that the chief city of his kingdom and the seat of his own palace might also be made the religious centre of the whole nation as a congregation of Jehovah, he first of all brought the ark of the covenant out of its place of concealment, and had it conveyed in a festal procession to Zion, and deposited there in a tent which had been specially prepared for it, as a place of worship for the whole congregation (2 Samuel 6). He then resolved to erect for the Lord in Jerusalem a temple fitted for His name; and the Lord gave him in return the promise of the eternal perpetuity of his throne (2 Samuel 7). To this there is appended a cursory account of David’s wars with the neighbouring nations, by which not only his own sovereignty, but the Israelitish kingdom of God, was raised into a commanding power among the nations and kingdoms of the world. In connection with all this, David still maintained his affection and fidelity towards the fallen royal family of Saul, and showed compassion towards the last remaining descendant of that family (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:1-13</reference>). <div eID="gen4286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4287" type="x-p"/> This account of the unfolding of the power and glory of the kingdom of Israel, through the instrumentality of David and during his reign, is so far arranged chronologically, that all the events and all the enterprises of David mentioned in this section occurred in the first half of his reign over the whole of the covenant nation. The chronological arrangement, however, is not strictly adhered to, so far as the details are concerned; but the standpoint of material resemblance is so far connected with it, that all the greater wars of David are grouped together in 2 Samuel 8 (see the introduction to 2 Samuel 8). It is obvious from this, that the plan which the historian adopted was first of all to describe the internal improvement of the Israelitish kingdom of God by David, and then to proceed to the external development of his power in conflict with the opposing nations of the world. David Anointed King over All Israel. Jerusalem Taken, and Made the Capital of the Kingdom. Victories over the Philistines. 2 Samuel 5.  <chapter eID="2Sam.4"/> <div eID="gen4287" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. IV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND when Sauls son heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, his hands were feeble <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">His Spirit, and Courage, and Strength failed him. This Phrase is used in the same sence, <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> 4. 4. <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 6. 9. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 13. 7. and 35. 3.</ns0:note>, and all the Israelites were troubled <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Because now they were unable to oppose <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and doubtful of obtaining his favour, now <ns0:hi>Abner</ns0:hi> their peace-maker was dead.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And Sauls son had two men <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> Captains of bands, the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> second.</ns0:note> other, Rechab, the sons of Rim<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon, a Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Of <ns0:hi>Ishbosheth</ns0:hi>'s own Tribe, whom therefore he trusted the more; and this gave them opportunity to execute their wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed design.</ns0:note>: (for Beeroth also was reckoned to Benjamin <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This is added as the reason why he called them <ns0:hi>Beerothites,</ns0:hi> because though <ns0:hi>Beeroth</ns0:hi> was now in the hands and Possession of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 31. 7. yet of right it belonged to the <ns0:hi>Benjamites, Iosh.</ns0:hi> 18. 25.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Yet,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>But.</ns0:hi> For this comes in to anticipate an Objection against what he had now said. It is true, saith he, <ns0:hi>the Beerothites fled,</ns0:hi> as others did, upon the overthrow of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and his Army; 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 31. 7. to a place called <ns0:hi>Gittaim;</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 4. 3. not that in <ns0:hi>Benjamin, Nehem.</ns0:hi> 11. 33. but some other place of that name more remote from the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> and so they were <ns0:hi>Gittaimites</ns0:hi> by their present Habitation; but <ns0:hi>Beerothites</ns0:hi> by their Original, and place of their Birth.</ns0:note> the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and were sojourners there until this day).</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And Jonathan, Sauls son, had a son <ns0:hi>that was</ns0:hi> lame of <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> feet <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This History is inserted as that which encouraged these men to this wicked Murder, because <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Family was now reduced to a low ebb; and if <ns0:hi>Ishbosheth</ns0:hi> was dispatched, there would be none left, but a lame Child, who was altoge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther unfit to manage the Kingdom, especially in so trouble<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />some a time as this was; and therefore the Crown must ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessarily come to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> by their act and deed; for which they promised themselves no small recompence.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> was five years old when the tidings came of <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">The slaugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter of</ns0:note> Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The place of that last and fatal Fight, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 29. 11.</ns0:note>, and his nurse took him up, and fled, and it came to pass as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />came lame; and his name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Merib-baal.</ns0:hi> 1 Chr. 8. 34. and 9. 40.</ns0:note> Mephibosheth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Called also <ns0:hi>Merib-baal,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 8. 34. See the notes on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 2. 8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chab and Baanah, went and came about the heat of the day to the house of Ish-bosheth, who lay on a bed at noon <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either, from discontent of mind, as <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi> did, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 21. 4. or from sloth and sensuality, as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> seems to have done, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 11. 2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And they came thither into the midst of the house <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>into the house:</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>midst</ns0:hi> is not always taken ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />actly, and Mathematically, but for any part within, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 48. 16. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 8. 22. <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 3. 17.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>as though</ns0:hi> they would have fetched wheat <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which was laid up in publick Granaries in the King's House, and was fetched thence by the Captains and Commanders of the Army for the Pay of their Soldiers, who, in those ancient times were not paid in Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney, but in Corn, as is well known. Upon this pretence they were admitted into the House, and so went from room to room, to the place where the King lay.</ns0:note>; and they smote him under the fifth <ns0:hi>rib;</ns0:hi> and Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chab and Baanah his brother escaped <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which was not difficult to do, when the King was left alone, either because he desired to compose himself to Rest o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Sleep: or, because his Guards, if he had any, were very small, and negligent, now at least, in his declining and forlorn Condition.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 For when they came into the house, he lay on his bed in his bed-chamber: and they smote him, and slew him, and beheaded him, and took his head, and gat them away through the plain <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the way from <ns0:hi>Mahanaim</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Hebron;</ns0:hi> which for the most part was a plain Country.</ns0:note> all night.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And they brought the head of Ish-bosheth un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to David to Hebron, and said to the king, Behold, the head of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, thine ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />my, which sought thy life <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To destroy it, or take it away; as this Phrase is used; 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 20. 1. and 23. 15. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>; and the LORD hath avenged my lord the king this day of Saul and of his seed <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> thought their Action not onely blameless, but Meritorious; because they had but executed Justice upon <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s House, and <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Enemies, and made way for <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> obtaining of his Rights. It may seem strange, they were not discouraged by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s punishing of the <ns0:hi>Amalekite</ns0:hi> for killing <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. and by his sharp Reproof of <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> for Murd ring <ns0:hi>Abner;</ns0:hi> but they thought the first Case much differing from theirs, because <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> was Anointed King by God: whereas, <ns0:hi>Ishbosheth</ns0:hi> was not, but was a meer Usurper: and for the latter, they thought that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s sharp words proceeded ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther from Art and Policy, than from any real dislike of the thing; which they judged, because <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> contented himself with words, and <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> did not onely go unpunished, but con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinued in his former Place and Power.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 ¶ And David answered Rechab, and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said unto them, <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> the LORD liveth, who hath re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deemed my soul out of all adversity <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Who hath hitherto delivered, and will deliver me from all mine Enemies. So that I needed not your wicked help in this way.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 When <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 1. 4, 15.</ns0:note> one told me, saying, Behold Saul is dead, (<ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> he was in his own eyes as a bringer, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> thinking to have brought good tidings) I took hold of him, and slew him in Ziklag, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> which was the wound I gave him for his tidings: or, to whom I was to give a reward for his tidings. So Gr.</ns0:note> who thought that I would have given him a reward for his tidings:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 How much more when wicked men have slain a righteous person <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">For so he was comparatively, and in respect of these men, having not deserved Death at their hands.</ns0:note> in his own house, upon his bed? Shall I not therefore now require his blood of your hand, and take you away from the earth?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:250" rendition="simple:additions" />12 And David commanded his young men <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Those of his Guard, who used to Execute Justice upon Malefactors at the Kings Command.</ns0:note>, and they slew them, and cut off their hands and their feet <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which had been most Instrumental in this Villany; their Hands to Cut off his Head, and their Feet to carry them away, and his Head with them.</ns0:note>, and hanged <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> up over the pool in Hebron <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">As Monuments of their Villany, and of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Abhorrency of it.</ns0:note>: but they took the head of Ish-bosheth, and buried <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 3. 32.</ns0:note> sepulchre of Abner in He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bron.</ns0:p>
